title: Demystifying Agent Skills: Why They Work - Until They Don't
authors: Zhiyuan Jiang, Fangrui Huang, Hanwen Xing, Xander Wu, Yipeng Gao, Rui Cao, Mengdi Wang, Shilong Liu, Yijiang Li
lab: Princeton, UC San Diego, Stanford, USC, Johns Hopkins (corresponding authors Mengdi Wang, Shilong Liu, Yijiang Li; Jiang worked on it as a Princeton intern)
date: August 2026 (arXiv v1, 14 August 2026; the only version so far)

code.title: no code released
code.note: The paper links no code or data. Its appendix mentions "released artifacts" but neither the arXiv page nor the LaTeX source gives an address (checked 3 October 2026). What can be inspected is the public benchmark task the paper's worked example comes from: SkillsBench's react-performance-debugging (Apache-2.0), whose service simulator, original checkout route, verifier and reference solution this page uses. About 15 minutes for the task, the simulator and the verifier

takeaway: First mechanistic account of SKILL.md: identical trajectories distilled into skills beat raw workflow memory by +6.06 points because skills act as procedural anchors (not knowledge injection), but they add a new 10% misapplication failure mode, and retrieval precision decouples from downstream task success.
verdict: Believe the direction: on most setups a distilled skill beats the same experience pasted in as workflow traces, and skills bring a misapplication failure of their own. Treat the sizes as provisional. The +6.06 points rests on one trial per arm on 88 Codex tasks and is not significant if a task's six triples are even slightly correlated; Gemini on Terminal-Bench-Pro shows the opposite; the mechanism shares come from one LLM judge that labels identical runs differently; and the retrieval "decoupling" uses a precision metric that mostly counts how many skills an agent opens.

resources.t: Equipping agents for the real world with Agent Skills
resources.n: the canonical description of the SKILL.md abstraction this paper dissects: progressive disclosure, the folder layout, and when to write a skill. Agent Skills became an open standard on 18 December 2025.
the public skill repository the paper cites as its reference skill-usage protocol; useful for seeing what production skills actually contain (about 20 minutes for the README and a couple of skills).

resources.t: SkillsBench: Benchmarking How Well Agent Skills Work Across Diverse Tasks
resources.n: the benchmark behind the retrieval study and the worked example; its own paired evaluation (87 tasks, 18 model and harness configurations) finds curated skills raise the average pass rate from 33.9% to 50.5%.

resources.t: SWE-Skills-Bench: Do Agent Skills Actually Help in Real-World Software Engineering?
resources.n: the sceptical counterpart: 39 of 49 public skills give no pass-rate gain on real repositories, and three hurt through version-mismatched guidance, which is this paper's misapplication mode seen from outside.
the workflow-memory representation this paper uses as its contrast arm, induced from past web-navigation trajectories.

resources.t: Terminal-Bench: Benchmarking Agents on Hard, Realistic Tasks in Command Line Interfaces
resources.n: the 89-task Terminal-Bench 2.0 used in two of the three benchmarks here, with its containerised tasks and test-based verification.
the task of the paper's paired example (Appendix A.3): the service latencies, the checkout route and the verifier that this page's replay reads from.

kb.n: the issue that covered this paper, in its Research section beside EnvHarness and Learn What's Left, under the week's harness theme.

kb.t: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models
kb.n: 2022-10: the acting loop these agents run; skills sit on top of it as reusable procedural memory.

kb.t: StateM: Reaching 95.3% Raw Accuracy, or a $15 Frontier Run, on Terminal-Bench 2.1 via Harness Scaling
kb.n: 2026-08: the same week's harness paper on a later Terminal-Bench, with versioned runbooks, a close cousin of a skill.

kb.t: Repo-To-Skill: Distilling GitHub Repositories Into AI4AI Skills
kb.n: skills distilled from repositories rather than from an agent's own trajectories.

kb.n: memory chosen per task, the retrieval side of this paper's lifecycle.
